claims.text: Surface segregation and selective oxidation of X govern formation and persistence of a protective oxide scale in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
A single-phase microstructure promotes uniform segregation of X to the alloy surface.
Uniform surface segregation of X enables formation of a continuous, adherent oxide.
Al-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys can form alumina through selective oxidation of Al.
Si-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys can form silica through selective oxidation of Si.
Multiphase alloys have heterogeneous elemental distributions and additional phase boundaries that cause uneven oxidation.
Uneven oxidation in multiphase alloys generates stresses that cause oxide cracking and spallation.
Microstructural homogeneity governs oxygen diffusion and reactive-element segregation.
A single-phase structure minimizes grain-boundary and interphase stresses.
Reduced grain-boundary and interphase stresses favor uniform oxide formation.
At high temperature, X preferentially migrates to the surface and oxidizes.
In single-phase alloys, selective oxidation of X produces a continuous, coherent oxide with low internal stress and good adhesion.
In multiphase alloys, oxidation is concentrated or nonuniform along phase boundaries.
Single-phase alloys will form more stable, uniform, adherent protective scales with less cracking and spallation than multiphase alloys under identical exposure conditions.
Unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide scales are typically observed in multiphase high-entropy alloys or when reactive-element surface segregation is insufficient.
The proposed mechanism applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and depends on whether the metallic state is single-phase or multiphase.
